notes: id="article"> November 16, 2026 Opening Remarks Chairman Kevin Warsh At the Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference, hosted by the Federal Reserve Board and the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, San Francisco, California Share --> --> --> --> --> --> Watch Live Mary, thank you, and welcome.
Everything I see reflects high expectations and the inquiring, forward-looking spirit that we need in the Federal Reserve System.

Yet, as Nick Bloom, Chad Jones, and their coauthors have pointed out, "Research productivity has fallen by an even larger amount." 2 The result: Productivity growth has fluctuated, and in recent quarters, it's been reasonably strong.
Long-run growth, I should note, is also a function of the rate of increase in the number of people producing new ideas and setting them in motion.
If idea generation broadens, growth could be sustained at a level substantially higher than the long-run average. 4 For all of that, however, humans should not be underestimated.

events.title: FOMC Member Waller Speaks
notes: Waller At “Navigating the Future of Banking and Payments,” The Clearing House Annual Conference 2026, New York, New York Share --> --> --> --> --> --> Watch Live Thank you for inviting me to return and speak today. 1 I am delighted to be here during a transformational time in payments.

Two years ago, I spoke at The Clearing House's annual conference, where I discussed the roles that the private sector and the Federal Reserve play in payments. 2 I argued that the public and private sectors have distinct but complementary roles.

The Federal Reserve can support these solutions by providing core payment and settlement infrastructure upon which the private sector can innovate, assessing potential risks to financial stability, and regularly engaging with the industry to better understand market challenges.
How will payment solutions integrate within and across platforms for tokenized assets to support the development of safe and efficient markets?

I expect continued dialogue between industry participants and the Fed will be helpful for thinking through considerations like cross-system connectivity and trust as the payment system evolves to support tokenized markets.

noteSrc.title: Waller, Considerations at the Intersection of Payments and Tokenized Markets

notes: id="article"> November 18, 2026 Investing in America’s Underserved Communities Governor Michael S.

I first saw that for myself 30 years ago, touring the South Bronx with Treasury Secretary Bob Rubin, where public–private partnerships were building housing, creating businesses and jobs, and making streets safer, block by block.
That progress has continued, and the strategies and partnerships we will be discussing today have been a major engine for that success.
If the economy evolves as I currently forecast, I expect it will be appropriate to raise rates further to achieve that goal on behalf of the American people.

notes: id="article"> November 19, 2026 Monetary Policy amid Frequent and Complex Shocks Vice Chair Philip N.
Just in the past few years, we have experienced a pandemic, a rapid rise in energy prices associated with geopolitical tensions, changes to trade policy, and a technological breakthrough.

When a shock moves the output gap and inflation in the same direction, our objectives are aligned, and policy actions taken to address one also support the other. 3 When a shock pushes them in opposite directions, there is a tradeoff.
If inflation expectations risk becoming unanchored, a stronger reaction to inflation is warranted.
In the future, advancements in productivity could exert downward pressure on inflation while continuing to support growth.

notes: id="article"> November 20, 2026 Opening Remarks Governor Christopher J.
The challenge is to prepare and present a monetary policy recommendation that will best promote the Federal Reserve's dual mandate of stable prices and maximum sustainable employment.

Like you, we will be examining publicly available data on economic and financial conditions and will apply our understanding of how monetary policy influences those conditions to render our best judgment of the policy stance that best furthers the Fed's goals.

Crucial to that decision will be clearly explaining the Committee's actions and intentions to the public—the same task that you will face later this morning, when you present your recommendations to our judges.
On December 8, my 18 FOMC colleagues and I will each present our view of the economic outlook, and on December 9, our view of the proper stance of monetary policy.

events.title: FOMC Member Cook Speaks
notes: This technology could bring a productivity boom unparalleled in generations. 2 At the same time, I worry deeply about our shared risks resulting from the technology, such as the specter of a painful labor market transition or cyber and financial-stability risks.
As with any major new technology, AI is likely to cause a shift in the labor market with jobs and job tasks being replaced by AI, and new jobs—many of which we cannot yet conceive of—being created.
The Federal Open Market Committee in September raised the target range for the federal funds rate to 3-3/4 to 4 percent to support a timelier return to the 2 percent objective.
Inflation has been above target for more than five and a half years, and every additional day poses greater risk that price- and wage-setters will adjust their inflation expectations upward.

Based on the most recent data available at the time, I saw risks to our mandate tilting toward inflation and noted that the longer inflation remains above target, the greater the probability that higher inflation will become entrenched in expectations.

noteSrc.title: Cook, The U.S. Economy in Global Context
